data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The urban heat island is fundamentally an optical phenomenon where the low albedo of dark urban surfaces causes disproportionate daytime heat storage, and the nighttime gap is larger in cities with more extensive impervious surface area coverage.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If high-albedo urban surfaces (e.g., white roofs) fail to significantly reduce nocturnal urban temperatures","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cross-city gap depends primarily on building geometry rather than total impervious area","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rural areas with similarly low albedo do not exhibit the same rapid nighttime cooling","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Low albedo surfaces in cities absorb a higher fraction of incoming solar radiation than reflective rural surfaces. This excess absorbed energy increases daytime heat storage in materials like asphalt. After sunset, this stored heat is released as longwave radiation, warming the air. The cross-city gap is larger in cities with greater impervious surface area and lower average albedo, as the total volume of heat stored and subsequently released scales with the extent of dark surfaces.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
